Sources — the snapshot, or the page a link was found on:
TYPO3 error page ("Oops, an error occurred")
TYPO3 shows its error page "Oops, an error occurred!": something on the page failed while rendering, usually a plugin or a content element. The exception is in the TYPO3 log.
The page shows an uncaught exception with stack trace — the development context shows it instead of the error page.
The page shows an uncaught exception of this class. The page or one of its content elements fails while rendering.
TYPO3 answers with its page-not-found message: the page does not exist under this URL, is hidden, or is not available in this language.
The page is protected: it is restricted to a frontend user group, or a page above it is.
No connection to the server — a wrong host, DNS, a firewall or credentials the server rejected.

The link answers exactly like the same URL without its arguments: the plugin they are meant for does not receive them, e.g. after it moved to another page or namespace.
The URL works only through a redirect. A sitemap should list the final URL, a link should point at it directly.
The URL works only through several redirects in a row. Each costs a request; the first one should point at the final URL.
More than ten redirects — almost always a loop between two rules.
The answer is larger than 50 MB and was not read.
The page answers, but names another URL as canonical — typically a page that shows the content of another page. Search engines index the canonical URL; the sitemap should not list this one.

The reference row: how the URL answered before the migration.

The URL already fails on the reference, so there is nothing to compare. It is listed in the sitemap search engines know, though. Possible causes: a detail page (news, job offer, product) listed in the page sitemap that only works with a record in its URL; an error in a plugin or content element; a page for logged-in users only.
Same path, same page or record.
The URL redirects to the same page or record. Nothing to do, unless a warning says otherwise.

The URL leads to the same page or record, but not in one step: the redirect points at a URL that redirects again, or at a page that names another URL as canonical. Point the redirect directly at the suggested final URL.

The URL answers with an error on the target and does not redirect. Possible causes: the page was moved or renamed without a redirect; it was not migrated, is hidden or not translated; its slug changed; an error on the target itself — check the status code.

The URL redirects, but ends in an error, a loop or too many redirects. Possible causes: the redirect target was deleted or moved; redirect rules lead into each other; rules for https, www or a trailing slash undo each other.

The URL answers with 200, but shows a different page, record or language. Possible causes: a redirect to a parent or start page; the slug is used by another page now; a language fallback shows the default language.

The URL answers with 200, but the markers needed for a comparison are missing. Possible causes: one environment does not render the page uid in the body tag or the record meta tag; a page template replaces the body tag.
A page from the target sitemap, requested to suggest redirect targets.
No complete answer within the timeout, also after the retries. The page may exist and only render slowly, e.g. right after a cache flush. Run the check again before treating it as missing.

The URL calls a page that shows content only with a parameter — the detail page of a plugin — without one. Whatever it answers, there is no page of its own to keep: the detail views are checked one by one. The page is marked in its page properties.

Possible causes: a detail page listed in the page sitemap that needs a record in its URL — the plugin fails without one; an exception in a plugin or content element; a database or configuration error on this environment. The TYPO3 log of this environment names the exception.
Possible causes: the page was moved or renamed without a redirect; it is hidden, deleted or not translated; the record of a detail page no longer exists.
Possible causes: the page is restricted to logged-in users; Basic Auth for this environment is missing or wrong; a web server rule blocks the request.
The server refused the request. Possible causes: a web server or firewall rule, rate limiting, or arguments in the URL the site does not accept.
The request got no HTTP answer. Possible causes: the host is unreachable, a DNS or certificate error, or a timeout — a higher --timeout may help.
More than one redirect before the final page. Point the first redirect directly at the final URL.
The chain contains a 302, 303 or 307. A permanent move should answer 301 or 308.
A deep URL redirects to a start page. Search engines often treat this as a soft 404.
The sitemap lists a URL that redirects. A sitemap should only contain final URLs.
The target page is in a different language than the reference page.
Several URLs render this page without a record marker — probably a detail page. Which record is shown cannot be compared.
The same record is rendered by more than one page. That is duplicate content.
A redirect leads to a TYPO3 shortcut page, which redirects again with 307. Point the redirect at the target of the shortcut.
The redirect ends on a page that names another URL as canonical — typically a page that shows the content of another page. Point the redirect at the canonical URL.
The sitemap lists a URL whose page names another URL as canonical. A sitemap should only contain canonical URLs.
The sitemap lists a page that shows content only with a parameter, called without one. Exclude it from the page sitemap.

The same page renders records under other URLs. If it shows content only with a record, this URL is a detail page without one and does not belong in the sitemap; if it shows a list as well, nothing is wrong.

Compares snapshot "%1$s" (before) with snapshot "%2$s" (after), requested on %3$s

A snapshot keeps the sitemaps of every language of a website at one point in time. It is the list of URLs every check works with, and it stays when the website changes: after a relaunch, the snapshot of the old site is the only record of the URLs search engines still send visitors to.
Choose a base URL of a configured site and find its sitemaps. The environment is suggested from the site configuration.
Select the languages, give the snapshot a label if you like, and import it.
Lock every snapshot you must not lose, e.g. the live state before a relaunch: the lock icon protects it from deletion, also by the cleanup command.
URLs outside the configured sites and scheduled imports need the command line: websitecheck:importsitemaps. Before the database is replaced, save the snapshots you need as files below.
What the status check is for

Finds every page of a website that does not work as it should: error pages, URLs that only answer through a redirect or name another URL as canonical, and — in the link check — plugin links whose arguments have no effect. The URL list comes from a snapshot and may be requested on another host: e.g. the sitemap of the development system, with news the live site does not have yet, checked against the live site.
Import a sitemap snapshot of the environment to check in the Sitemaps module.
Compose the check below and run the command on the command line. Every URL is requested, which can take a while.
Reload this page and review the results: filter by environment and problems, mark findings as reviewed and add a note where needed.
Moved URLs and redirects are the job of the migration check: it compares two environments page by page.
What the migration check is for

Makes sure a relaunch loses no URL: every URL search engines know from the old website has to lead to the same page or record on the new one — directly or through a redirect. Pages and records are recognised by what they are, not by their URL, so a redirect to the wrong content is found as well. Where a redirect is missing, the module suggests where it should point.
Before the switch: import the sitemaps of the live site and lock the snapshot.
Import a snapshot of the new site, e.g. staging, compose the check below and run it. Repeat after every change to the new site.
Review the results: missing redirects per page and record, with a suggested target where one can be derived.

After the switch: import a snapshot of the new live site and reuse the reference results of the last run — the old site no longer answers. Export the last run beforehand if the database gets replaced.
Both sites have to render the page and record markers described in the documentation; without them pages cannot be compared.

Requests the paths of the snapshot on another host. Example: the snapshot was taken on www.example.com, the host is staging.example.com — you see before the switch whether every URL search engines know answers on the new system. Or the other way round: a sitemap provider only exists on staging while the pages are live already. Redirects and content are compared by the migration check.

Results are stored per environment label and URL; a new run with the same label replaces them. Use one label per environment and check, e.g. "staging" for the status check and "staging-links" for the link check of the same site.

A shape is the path of a link plus the names of its arguments. /news/detail?tx_news_pi1[news]=12 and …[news]=13 share one shape, so a list of a hundred news items is checked with this many links, not a hundred.
The URLs of the old site as search engines know them. Take the locked live snapshot from before the switch — a newer live snapshot already lists the URLs of the new site.

Before the switch, both sites answer and every run requests both. After it, www.example.com shows the new site: a run named "relaunch" from before the switch still knows how every old URL answered, and a run "after-relaunch" reuses those rows and only requests the new site.
They name the two sides in the results, e.g. "live" and "staging". After the switch both are live: "live-before" and "live-after" keep them apart.
Says where the snapshot comes from. The migration check suggests the locked live snapshot as reference and the newest staging, development or local one as target — so tag live snapshots as live.
The name the checks use to find the snapshot, e.g. "live-before-relaunch". It has to be unique. Left empty, it is the host and the time, e.g. "www.example.com 2026-01-31 14:05".

A database that is replaced — e.g. by a fresh import of the live database — takes every snapshot and every stored check result with it. A saved file brings them back, and it moves them to another installation, e.g. from staging to the new live system. The files are the same as those of websitecheck:exportsnapshots.
Snapshots and migration check runs saved to %1$s. Reading a file in skips what is already here; a label used by another record stops it. Keep the directory out of version control.
No saved files yet. Save a snapshot with the button in its header, or a migration check run in the migration check module.
Saving to files is switched off. Set an archive directory in Settings → Extension Configuration → ot_websitecheck, e.g. data/websitecheck, to save snapshots here before the database is replaced.
A label in this file is used by another record here. Rename or delete that record, or read the file in with websitecheck:importsnapshots --label-suffix.
"%1$s" is deleted from the directory. It may be the only copy of these snapshots.
Saves this snapshot to the archive directory, so it survives a replaced database.
Saves this run with its results and the snapshots it compared — after the switch, its reference results can no longer be requested.
The run was saved as %1$s, with the snapshots it compared. Read it in from the Sitemaps module.

What the checks report, whether you can fix it in the backend or have to pass it on, and what to do. Every finding in the other modules links to its entry here.
store the sitemaps of a site as a snapshot. Every check reads its URLs from a snapshot, and a snapshot stays when the site changes — before a relaunch, lock the one of the live site.
request every URL of a snapshot on one environment: which ones fail, show an error page or only work through a redirect.
compare two environments, usually the live site and a relaunch: does every old URL still lead to the same page or record?
For integrators: how to fix it
The URL works on the reference, usually the live site, but answers with an error on the target and does not redirect. Visitors and search engines that know the old URL end on an error page.

Create a redirect from the old path to the page that replaces it, in the Redirects module. Where the module shows a suggested target, that is the same page or record on the target. If the page should exist under the old URL, check whether it is hidden, not translated, or has a changed URL segment.
A redirect ends in an error
There is a redirect, but where it leads fails: an error page, a loop between two redirects, or more redirects than are followed.

Open the redirect chain shown in the row and correct the target of the redirect, in the Redirects module. A redirect that is not listed there comes from the webserver configuration — pass it on to the integrator.
Migration check: Redirect not final, Redirect chain, Shortcut page in the chain · Status check: Through several redirects, Too many redirects

The right page is reached, but not in one step: the redirect points at a URL that redirects again — often a page that was moved later, or a shortcut page, which redirects again by itself. Every step costs time, and search engines carry less over to the new URL.
Change the first redirect so it points at the suggested final URL, in the Redirects module. A redirect that is not listed there comes from the webserver configuration — pass it on to the integrator.
The redirect answers with 302, 303 or 307. Search engines keep the old URL in their index, because the move is announced as temporary.
Set the status code of the redirect to 301 in the Redirects module. A shortcut page always redirects with 307 — point the redirect past it, at its target.
Migration check: Other content, Redirect to start page

The URL answers, but with a different page, record or language than before — for example after a redirect to a parent or start page, or because another page uses the URL now. A redirect to the start page is treated by search engines like a page that no longer exists.

Point the redirect at the page that replaces the old one, in the Redirects module; a suggested target is shown where one is certain. If another page took over the URL on purpose, mark the row as reviewed.
The page is in another language
The target page is in a different language than the reference — usually because a translation is missing and a fallback shows the default language.
Translate the page or record, or redirect the URL to a page in its language.
A page names another URL as canonical
Migration check: Canonical URL differs, Sitemap URL not canonical · Status check: Canonical URL elsewhere

Every page tells search engines under which URL it should be indexed — its canonical URL. A page with "Show Content from this page" names the page whose content it shows, and a page can name another one in its SEO properties. That is correct; the same content is indexed once. But such a page does not belong in the sitemap, and a redirect should not end on it.

A redirect that ends on such a page: point it at the canonical URL, in the Redirects module. A sitemap that lists such pages: pass it on to the integrator — the sitemap configuration has to leave them out.
A detail page is called without a record
Migration check: Detail page without record, Sitemap lists a detail page, Page also renders records · Status check: Detail page without record

The detail page of a plugin — a product, a job, a news item — shows content only with a record in its URL. Called without one, it shows a list, an empty page or an error. Such a URL is no page of its own: nobody needs it, and nothing is lost when it fails. The detail views with their records are checked one by one.

Nothing to do in the content. The sitemap should not list the page: pass it on to the integrator. Where the site has a page property for it ("Page requires a parameter" or similar), set it on every detail page.
The sitemap lists a URL that redirects
Migration check: Sitemap URL redirects · Status check: Only through a redirect

A sitemap should only contain the URLs search engines are meant to index. A URL that redirects makes them request two URLs for one page. In the link check, a link in the content points at a URL that redirects.

A link in the content: change it to the final URL. A URL in the sitemap: TYPO3 builds the sitemap from the pages, so a redirect there usually comes from the server configuration, e.g. a rule for trailing slashes — pass it on to the integrator.
Status check: an HTTP status other than 200, a TYPO3 error page or exception, Response too large

The URL answers with an error. 404 or "page not found": the page does not exist under this URL, is hidden or not translated. Access denied: the page is restricted to a user group. An exception or "Oops, an error occurred!": a plugin or content element fails while rendering.
Not found or access denied: check the page in the page tree — visibility, translation, access. An exception: note the URL and pass it on to the integrator; the details are in the TYPO3 log.
Migration check: Timeout · Status check: Timeout, No connection

The page did not answer within the time limit, also after the retries — or the server could not be reached at all. Slow is not missing: a page that renders for the first time after a cache flush can take long.
Run the check again. A page that keeps timing out, and every connection error, goes to the integrator.
Migration check: Identity unknown, Record unknown

The migration check compares pages by what they are — page and record — not by their URL. For that, the site has to name them in its HTML. Without these markers, it cannot tell whether a URL still shows the same page.
Pass it on to the integrator: the markers are added in the templates of the site — on every environment that is compared, the live site included.
A record is shown on several pages
The same record is rendered by more than one detail page. Search engines find the same content under several URLs.
Pass it on to the integrator: one detail page per record type should render the records, and the others should link to it or name it as canonical.
Status check of links: Link arguments have no effect

A link carries arguments for a plugin — a record, a page of results — but the page answers exactly as without them. The plugin does not receive them, e.g. because it moved to another page. Visitors get a plausible looking wrong page.
Pass it on to the integrator, with the page the link was found on: the template or plugin setting that builds the link has to point at the page with the plugin.
A URL was broken before already
The URL fails on the reference already — the site the comparison starts from. Nothing was lost in the migration; the old sitemap listed a broken URL.
Nothing to do for the migration. If the URL matters, e.g. because it is linked from outside, give it a redirect to a fitting page.
Terms the checks use, and where to find the matching settings in TYPO3. Field names are those of the page properties.

A list of the URLs of a website that search engines are meant to index, e.g. under /sitemap.xml. TYPO3 creates it from the pages and — per plugin — from records such as news. A page is left out when its "Index this page" switch is off or it has its own canonical link.

A copy of all sitemaps of a website at one point in time, stored in the Sitemaps module. Every check takes its URLs from a snapshot. A locked snapshot cannot be deleted — before a relaunch, lock the one of the live site.

One installation of the same website: live is the public one, staging the copy for testing and approval, development and local the ones developers work on. They often differ in content and configuration.

The number a server answers a request with. 200: the page works. 301 and 308: moved permanently. 302 and 307: moved temporarily. 404 and 410: not found. 403: access denied. 500 and above: an error on the server, often in TYPO3 itself.

The answer "this page is elsewhere now", with the new URL. Editors maintain redirects in the Redirects module, where the extension redirects is installed; the webserver can redirect as well, by rules only the integrator changes. A move should be permanent (301), so search engines carry the old URL's ranking over.
Several redirects in a row before a page answers. Each costs time and some of what search engines carry over. The first redirect should point at the final URL directly.

The URL under which a page wants to be indexed, named in its HTML. Where the same content is reachable under several URLs, search engines index it only under this one. TYPO3 sets it to the page itself, unless the page names another one: page properties, tab SEO, field "Canonical link". A page with its own canonical link is left out of the sitemap.

A page can show the content elements of another page: page properties, tab Appearance, section "Replace Content", field "Show Content from this page". It answers under its own URL, but names the other page as canonical. TYPO3 still lists it in the sitemap — the integrator can leave such pages out.
A page of the type "Shortcut" shows no content of its own and redirects to another page — always with 307, a temporary redirect. A redirect should point past it, at its target.
The part of the URL that belongs to a page, e.g. /about-us. It is set in the page properties, tab General, field "URL Segment". Changing it changes the URL — without a redirect, the old one is lost.
The number TYPO3 identifies a page by, shown in square brackets after the title, e.g. [48]. Copy it into the search of the page tree to find the page.

Content that is not a page — a news item, a product, a job — is a record. A plugin shows it on a detail page, whose URL carries the record, e.g. /news/my-article. The same page without a record shows a list, an empty page or an error.
Page properties, tab SEO, switch "Index this page": switched off, search engines are asked not to index the page, and it is left out of the sitemap.
When a page or record has no translation, TYPO3 can show the default language instead — depending on the site configuration. The URL works, but in the wrong language.

Hidden details in the HTML of a page that name the page ID and, on a detail page, the record. The migration check compares pages by them. The integrator adds them to the templates; editors see nothing of them.
